question: Do simulated runs on weekend days carry a different number of passengers than runs on weekdays?
method: Welch t-test (+ Mann-Whitney U as a robustness check)
result: weekend mean 499.7 vs weekday mean 536.1 passengers/run; difference -36.4 (95% CI -73.4 to +0.6); p = 0.054; Mann-Whitney p = 0.217
interpretation: The difference (-36.4 passengers/run) is not statistically distinguishable from zero at the 5% level (the interval includes 0): no weekday effect can be claimed from this sample.
limitation: Synthetic, sampled simulation: the effect reflects the generator's assumptions, not real passenger behaviour; association only, not causation.

question: Do runs inside peak travel periods carry more passengers than other runs?
result: peak mean 638.8 vs other 498.1 passengers/run; difference +140.7 (95% CI +96.1 to +185.3); p < 0.001
interpretation: Peak-period runs show a medium difference (d = 0.59); consistent with the peak-period demand uplift the simulation builds in.
limitation: Synthetic, sampled simulation: the effect reflects the generator's assumptions, not real passenger behaviour; association only, not causation.

question: Is seat occupancy higher on runs inside peak travel periods?
result: peak mean 0.846 vs other 0.709; difference +0.137 (95% CI +0.107 to +0.167); p < 0.001
interpretation: A medium effect (d = 0.72); occupancy is bounded at 100%, so differences compress at the top.
limitation: Synthetic, sampled simulation: the effect reflects the generator's assumptions, not real passenger behaviour; association only, not causation.

question: Is the share of fully cancelled bookings related to how far ahead the booking was made?
metric: booking-based cancellation rate by lead-time bucket
method: chi-square test of independence (+ Cramer's V)
result: rate rises from 9.3% (0-3 days) to 21.4% (61-120 days); chi-square = 2,448, dof = 4, p < 0.001
interpretation: Strong statistical evidence of association with a small effect (V = 0.110); longer lead times go with higher cancellation in this dataset (the simulation builds in such a pattern).
limitation: Synthetic, sampled simulation: the effect reflects the generator's assumptions, not real passenger behaviour; association only, not causation. Bookings are the unit, so passengers within a booking are not double counted.

question: Does seat occupancy differ between travel classes?
metric: occupancy of each simulated train-class run
method: Kruskal-Wallis H test (rank-based; occupancy is bounded and skewed)
interpretation: Classes differ with a small effect; class-level occupancy comparisons are meaningful, but see the limitation on independence.
limitation: Synthetic, sampled simulation: the effect reflects the generator's assumptions, not real passenger behaviour; association only, not causation. Class-runs of the same train run share a date, so they are not fully independent; the 1A class has few runs.

question: Does the arrival delay differ between seasons?
unit_of_analysis: simulated run with a recorded delay
interpretation: No detectable seasonal difference in arrival delay.
limitation: Synthetic, sampled simulation: the effect reflects the generator's assumptions, not real passenger behaviour; association only, not causation. Delays are simulated; 23 runs with a missing delay are excluded, not imputed.

question: Does the share of on-time runs (arrival delay <= 15 minutes) differ between seasons?
unit_of_analysis: simulated run with a recorded delay
method: chi-square test of independence (+ Cramer's V)
result: chi-square = 4.6, dof = 3, p = 0.206; OTP by season: Monsoon 73.1%, Post-Monsoon 79.0%, Summer 78.4%, Winter 70.6%
interpretation: No detectable seasonal difference in on-time performance.
limitation: Synthetic, sampled simulation: the effect reflects the generator's assumptions, not real passenger behaviour; association only, not causation. Expected counts per cell are modest (about 745 runs).

question: Is there a linear trend in bookings per simulated run across the 24 months?
metric: bookings per simulated run, by month
method: ordinary least squares slope on the month index (in-sample description)
result: slope +2.36 bookings/run per month (95% CI +0.23 to +4.49); R-squared = 0.19; p = 0.032
interpretation: A straight line summarises these 24 months; seasonality is not modelled, so it is a description of the period, not a trend in demand.
limitation: Synthetic, sampled simulation. In-sample description only: it is NOT extrapolated and is not a forecast. 24 points, with seasonal structure, are too few for trend claims.

question: How strongly is the fare per passenger related to route distance?
metric: booking fare per passenger vs route distance (km)
limitation: Synthetic data: fares are generated by a distance-and-class formula, so this relationship is mechanical, not a discovery about pricing; class mix also contributes.

question: Are busier runs associated with longer arrival delays?
metric: passengers per run vs arrival delay (minutes)
unit_of_analysis: simulated run with a recorded delay
limitation: Synthetic, sampled simulation: the effect reflects the generator's assumptions, not real passenger behaviour; association only, not causation. Per assumption A-20 the generator ties delays to season, distance and train type, not to demand, so the absence of an association is expected.

question: Does the waitlist clearance rate differ between travel classes?
metric: share of initially waitlisted passengers who finished Confirmed or RAC
method: chi-square test of independence (+ Cramer's V)
result: chi-square = 72, dof = 5, p < 0.001; clearance by class: 1A 18.2%, 2A 12.8%, 3A 19.8%, SL 20.4%, CC 25.6%, 2S 17.6%
interpretation: Classes differ with a negligible effect (V = 0.044).
limitation: Synthetic, sampled simulation: the effect reflects the generator's assumptions, not real passenger behaviour; association only, not causation. Passengers are the unit but they cluster within bookings and runs, so the p-value is optimistic; rely on the effect size and the intervals.
